findings.evidence: features/007-prune-skill/007-prune-skill-prd.md:R8 + AC-8 — R8 names lock-file concurrency control with three cases (no lock / fresh lock / stale lock) and a clock-skew tolerance (lock-body timestamp cross-checked against filesystem mtime, with a 60-second tolerance window). AC-8 enumerates the three cases plus the `--force-unlock` y/N confirm-prompt. Two unaddressed edge cases: (i) **`--force-unlock` race window.** The user runs `/prune --force-unlock` at 14:30 (lock removed). At 14:30:01, the cron-fire path enters and finds no lock; it creates a new lock and proceeds. At 14:30:02, the user manually fires `/prune` (intending to start a fresh run after force-unlocking) and hits the cron's freshly-created lock — refused with the in-flight sentinel. The user's mental model is 'I just unlocked; why is it locked?'. The race is real and the PRD does not name how to handle it. (ii) **Cron-host clock far in the past or future.** R8 names a 60-second clock-skew tolerance, which covers minor NTP drift. But a cron host whose clock is hours wrong (rare but documented in real-world incident reports — e.g. battery-backup failure on a NAS clock) would (a) write a far-past lock timestamp that triggers the stale-lock-overwrite path immediately on a fresh second invocation, OR (b) write a far-future lock timestamp that NEVER triggers the stale path. Both cases produce silent wrong outcomes — case (a) lets two concurrent runs proceed; case (b) makes the lock un-removable except via `--force-unlock`. The 60-second tolerance is too narrow to detect the failure mode (which is hours-scale skew, not seconds-scale).
findings.claim: Coverage gap — R8's lock-concurrency machinery has two unaddressed cases. Case (i) `--force-unlock` race produces a confused user state: the user expects force-unlock to enable their next `/prune` invocation, but the cron path can capture the freed lock between unlock and re-invoke. Case (ii) clock-skew at hours-scale silently invalidates the lock semantics — either letting concurrent runs proceed (past-clock case) or making the lock un-removable (future-clock case). The 60-second tolerance the PRD names handles NTP-drift scale, not the actual failure mode (battery-failed clock or misconfigured timezone offset).
findings.proposed_change: Extend R8 with explicit handling for both edge cases: **(i) `--force-unlock` race.** After a force-unlock removes the lock, the skill emits a chat-line *'[lock cleared at {timestamp}; re-invoke /prune within 5 minutes to start a fresh run]'* AND writes a one-line marker file at `admin/scratch/prune-{YYYY-Q}.unlock-marker` containing the unlock timestamp. The next `/prune` invocation reads the marker; if its timestamp is within 5 minutes of now, the invocation has priority — any concurrent cron-path that would otherwise create a lock between the unlock and the re-invoke must defer. The marker is consumed (deleted) by the next manual `/prune` invocation OR auto-expires after 5 minutes (whichever first). **(ii) Clock-skew at hours-scale.** Bound the clock-skew tolerance to a sane range — if the lock-body timestamp is more than 24 hours in the past (older than any real run could have started) OR more than 1 hour in the future (no real lock acquisition is in the future), treat the lock as corrupt: refuse with *'Lock file at admin/scratch/prune-{YYYY-Q}.lock has implausible timestamp {ts} (compared to current time {now}). Inspect the lock file by hand and use --force-unlock if appropriate.'* The 24-hour past bound covers the battery-failed-clock case; the 1-hour future bound covers misconfigured timezone offsets. Update AC-8 to enumerate both edge cases.
